awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Improving the reliability of the United States' energy grid by predicting transformer failures
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Technology Transfer Phase I project seeks to develop an electronic partial discharge (PD) monitoring system that addresses the unmet need for noninvasive, cost-effective continuous PD monitoring. Over two-thirds of electrical transformers in the United States are at or past their expected lifespan, leaving the energy grid at risk of catastrophic failure. Current technologies for monitoring transformer health are expensive to operate, invasive, or require the use of additional resources (e.g., off-site analysis equipment). Because of the resources and human-power required of these existing tools, particularly those that require testing at the transformer site, PD monitoring occurs infrequently (i.e., annually) and only identifies PD after it has occurred. The technology to be developed offers risk mitigation by enabling electric companies to make informed decisions about transformer maintenance, utilizing PD detection and prediction capabilities. This technology will have unmatched value in strategic planning, where plans for transformer maintenance and replacement are based on continuous health information. Overall, the technology will positively impact all Americans that use electronics regularly, and could ultimately serve as a platform that can monitor PD in a variety of electrically insulated components, such as switchgears, inverters, generators, and electric motors. 

The intellectual merit of this project involves a novel, patented technology that allows the collection of high-quality data at a rate two orders of magnitude above that provided by traditional sensors, circumventing existing bandwidth and signal-to-noise limitations. This innovation significantly extends the sensor’s operational range, improving the accuracy of PD detection. The volume of data captured by this new sensor design will also provide a foundation for training models on the physical and application-specific elements of equipment failures, enabling more accurate detection of anomalies and prediction of specific failure types. In Phase I, R&D will be conducted to develop a prototype that meets the requirements for non-invasive function (i.e., installation on the transformer’s external wires) while maintaining a high level of sensitivity and data capture. During the program, the following objectives will be pursued: 1) assessment of bandwidth, sensitivity, and signal-to-noise characteristics at lab scale; 2) translation of benchtop characteristics to the bucket transformer use case; and 3) enhancement of the material platform, signal processing, and read-out interface.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Transformers are essential to the electric grid, supplying power to communities, businesses, renewable energy projects, data centers, and manufacturing facilities. As equipment ages and electricity demand grows, identifying developing faults before they cause outages becomes increasingly important. Existing monitoring approaches often provide periodic snapshots or require separate instruments to assess different aspects of transformer condition. Through this NSF Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project, Magnefy investigated an affordable, non-invasive magnetic sensing platform with machine learning analytics to support earlier identification of electrical and insulation problems.

The project addressed three technical areas: development and characterization of the hybrid sensing platform; integration of data acquisition, signal processing, and diagnostic analytics; and validation through controlled transformer testing. The research combined semiconductor sensor development, broadband electronics, real-time processing, and transformer diagnostics. Its principal outcome was an integrated prototype capable of capturing low-frequency harmonics and high-frequency partial discharge (PD) activity through accessible external conductors. PD consists of localized electrical discharges that can indicate insulation defects. Tracking these signals can provide information about developing problems and support maintenance decisions.

The original concept envisioned placing a thermally stable, gallium-based Hall-effect sensor inside the transformer tank. During Phase I, market research and feedback from GE Vernova identified practical barriers to internal installation and favored external mounting on transformer ground wires. This approach simplifies retrofitting existing equipment but requires greater sensitivity because discharge signals can weaken along their propagation paths. The team therefore investigated how to preserve broad frequency coverage while improving detection of small discharge signals at external monitoring locations.

The team fabricated and characterized gallium nitride Hall-effect sensors with different sizes and geometries, establishing trade-offs among sensitivity, resistance, capacitance, and bandwidth. These studies demonstrated MHz-range operation while identifying sensitivity limitations for external PD detection using a Hall-effect sensor alone. To address this challenge, the team developed a hybrid architecture combining a Hall-effect or tunneling magnetoresistance element for lower-frequency measurements with a planar induction coil for high-frequency signals. Configurable electronics combined their complementary responses, providing measurement coverage from approximately 30 Hz to 80 MHz within a common sensing platform.

Controlled transformer testing demonstrated measurement of both harmonics and PD. The magnetoresistive configuration captured harmonics through the nineteenth order, while the Hall-effect configuration captured through the seventeenth order. In the 5–10 MHz band, the hybrid sensor achieved approximately 8.4 times the sensitivity of a reference commercial high-frequency current transformer. Calibrated injection tests demonstrated detection down to 10 picocoulombs at the coupling-capacitor ground and 50 picocoulombs at evaluated bushing-adapter and tank-ground locations. These results established the importance of installation-dependent signal coupling and informed sensor-placement guidance. The reported sensor unit cost was approximately one-sixth that of the reference instrument.

A synchronized, four-channel acquisition system operated at 250 million samples per second. Real-time processing reduced interference, selected candidate discharge events, and captured waveforms for analysis. Improved synchronization with the power-frequency cycle produced phase-resolved discharge patterns consistent with a commercial reference instrument. These patterns help distinguish different discharge mechanisms. Measurements were transmitted through a cellular gateway to cloud-based analytics for remote review. Preliminary surge testing up to 3 kilovolts produced no observed damage or loss of operation, supporting further development for outdoor deployment.

Machine learning models used waveform characteristics and phase-resolved patterns to distinguish discharge activity from residual noise and classify evaluated discharge sources. The pipeline achieved 99 percent classification accuracy under controlled test conditions. Phase I also established a PD-specific Dynamic Health Index based on discharge type, amplitude, and repetition rate, connecting measured activity with preliminary insulation-condition assessments and engineer-reviewed maintenance recommendations. These outcomes demonstrate technical feasibility; performance on naturally occurring defects and across diverse operating environments remains to be validated.

The project’s intellectual contribution is a complementary sensing and processing architecture that captures electrical operating behavior and insulation-related transients through non-invasive measurements. Its potential broader impact is to support the energy transition by safeguarding aging transformer infrastructure and enabling power infrastructure expansion. Accessible continuous monitoring could help operators prioritize targeted maintenance, extend asset service life, and plan refurbishment or replacement. Better condition information could support strategic capital allocation, helping operators direct resources toward upgrades and capacity investments needed for reliable growth.

Beyond transformers, the platform could be adapted to switchgear, power converters, motors, generators, and cables. With asset-specific validation, it could establish a shared risk-intelligence data layer across power infrastructure, translating condition measurements into maintenance priorities and capital-planning insights. Phase II will address final sensor selection, calibration, environmental qualification, manufacturability, expanded diagnostic datasets, and naturally occurring PD detection. Extended deployments will evaluate false-alarm rates, reliability, and operational usefulness. Phase I provides an integrated technical foundation and a defined research path toward broader infrastructure monitoring and better-informed asset management.
